prompt:
Let $G$ be a finite group having the property that for every choice of two subgroups $X\subseteq G$ and $Y\subseteq G$, either $X\cap Y=1$ or $X\subseteq Y$ or $Y\subseteq X$.

(i) If $H\subseteq G$, show that either $|H|$ is a prime power or else that $|H|$ and $|G:H|$ are relatively prime.

(ii) If $1<N\trianglelefteq G$, prove that $G/N$ is nilpotent.

(iii) If $N\trianglelefteq G$ and $N\neq G$, show that $N$ is nilpotent.
answer:
(i) If $|H|$ is not a prime power, each Sylow $p$-subgroup $P$ of $G$ meeting $H$ in a Sylow subgroup $
e1$ of $H$ must lie in $H$. (ii) Two Sylow subgroups $P/N,Q/N$ for different primes would give incomparable $P,Q$ with $P\cap Q=N
e1$; so $G/N$ is a $p$-group. (iii) For $1
e P\in\mathrm{Syl}_p(N)$, Frattini gives $G=NN_G(P)$, and $N_G(P)\cap N
e1$ forces $N\subseteq N_G(P)$, so every Sylow subgroup of $N$ is normal.

solutions.title: Comparability of subgroups
solutions.body:
**(i)** Suppose $|H|$ is not a prime power, and let $p$ be a prime dividing $|H|$. Let $Q\in\mathrm{Syl}_p(H)$ and choose $P\in\mathrm{Syl}_p(G)$ with $Q\subseteq P$. Then $P\cap H\supseteq Q
e1$, so $P\subseteq H$ or $H\subseteq P$. The latter would make $H$ a $p$-group, contrary to assumption. Hence $P\subseteq H$, so the full $p$-part of $|G|$ divides $|H|$ and $p
mid|G:H|$. As this holds for every prime $p$ dividing $|H|$, $\gcd(|H|,|G:H|)=1$.

**(ii)** We show $G/N$ is a $p$-group for some prime $p$ (or trivial), hence nilpotent. Suppose distinct primes $p,q$ divide $|G/N|$, and take $P,Q$ with $N\subseteq P,Q$, $P/N\in\mathrm{Syl}_p(G/N)$, $Q/N\in\mathrm{Syl}_q(G/N)$, both nontrivial. Then $(P\cap Q)/N\subseteq P/N\cap Q/N=1$, so $P\cap Q=N
e1$. Hence $P\subseteq Q$ or $Q\subseteq P$; but $P\subseteq Q$ would make the nontrivial $p$-group $P/N$ a subgroup of the $q$-group $Q/N$, impossible, and symmetrically. Contradiction.

**(iii)** A finite group is nilpotent iff all its Sylow subgroups are normal. Let $P\in\mathrm{Syl}_p(N)$ with $P
e1$. By the Frattini argument, $G=N\,N_G(P)$. Now $N_G(P)\cap N\supseteq P
e1$, so $N_G(P)\subseteq N$ or $N\subseteq N_G(P)$. In the first case $G=N\,N_G(P)=N$, contradicting $N
e G$. So $N\subseteq N_G(P)$, i.e. $P	rianglelefteq N$. Thus every Sylow subgroup of $N$ is normal and $N$ is nilpotent. ∎

prompt: Let $R$ be a ring, let $V$ be a right $R$-module, and suppose that $V=V_1\dotplus V_2\dotplus V_3\dotplus\cdots$ is the (internal) direct sum of its submodules $V_1,V_2,V_3,\ldots$. Show that $V$ is an Artinian module if and only if each $V_i$ is Artinian and only finitely many of the $V_i$'s are nonzero.
answer: ($\Rightarrow$) Submodules of Artinian modules are Artinian, and the chain $W_i=V_i\dotplus V_{i+1}\dotplus\cdots$ stabilizes, forcing $V_i=0$ for large $i$. ($\Leftarrow$) Induction on the number of nonzero summands, using that an extension of an Artinian module by an Artinian module is Artinian.

solutions.title: Tail chain and extensions
solutions.body:
**($\Rightarrow$)** Submodules of $V_i$ are submodules of $V$, so each $V_i$ inherits the descending chain condition. For $i\ge1$ let $W_i=V_i\dotplus V_{i+1}\dotplus\cdots$. Then $W_1\supseteq W_2\supseteq\cdots$ is a descending chain, so there is $n$ with $W_i=W_{i+1}$ for all $i\ge n$. But $W_i=V_i\dotplus W_{i+1}$ is a direct sum, so $W_i=W_{i+1}$ forces $V_i=V_i\cap W_{i+1}=0$. Hence $V_i=0$ for all $i\ge n$.

**($\Leftarrow$)** We may assume $V=V_1\dotplus\cdots\dotplus V_n$. Recall: if $W\subseteq V$ with $W$ and $V/W$ Artinian, then $V$ is Artinian. (Proof: given $U_1\supseteq U_2\supseteq\cdots$, the chains $U_k\cap W$ and $(U_k+W)/W$ stabilize, say for $k\ge k_0$; then for $k\ge k_0$, $U_{k+1}\subseteq U_k$ with $U_{k+1}\cap W=U_k\cap W$ and $U_{k+1}+W=U_k+W$, and the modular law gives $U_k=U_k\cap(U_{k+1}+W)=U_{k+1}+(U_k\cap W)=U_{k+1}$.)

Induct on $n$; $n=1$ is given. For $n>1$ let $W=V_1\dotplus\cdots\dotplus V_{n-1}$, Artinian by induction. Then $V/W\cong V_n$ is Artinian, so $V$ is Artinian. ∎

prompt:
Let $f(x)\in\mathbb{Q}[x]$ be a polynomial of degree $5$ over the rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$ that is not solvable by radicals, and let $S$ be the splitting field of $f(x)$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ which is contained in the complex numbers.

(i) Show that there exists at most one subfield $E$ of $S$ such that $|E:\mathbb{Q}|=2$.

(ii) If $\alpha,\beta\in S$ are irrational elements which satisfy $\alpha^2\in\mathbb{Q}$ and $\beta^2\in\mathbb{Q}$, prove that $\alpha\beta\in\mathbb{Q}$.
answer: (i) $G=\mathrm{Gal}(S/\mathbb{Q})$ is a nonsolvable subgroup of $S_5$, hence $A_5$ or $S_5$, which have $0$ resp. $1$ subgroups of index 2. (ii) Then $\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]=\mathbb{Q}[\beta]$, so $\beta=a\alpha+b$; squaring forces $b=0$, so $\alpha\beta=a\alpha^2\in\mathbb{Q}$.

solutions.title: Nonsolvable subgroups of $S_5$
solutions.body:
**(i)** $S/\mathbb{Q}$ is Galois with group $G$, which acts faithfully on the $\le5$ roots of $f$, so $G\le S_5$. Since $f$ is not solvable by radicals, $G$ is not solvable (Galois).

*Claim: $G=A_5$ or $G=S_5$.* By Burnside's $p^aq^b$ theorem, $|G|$ is divisible by $2$, $3$ and $5$, so $30\mid|G|$, and $|G|\mid120$; so $|G|\in\{30,60,120\}$. A group of order $30$ is solvable (a group of order $2m$ with $m$ odd has a normal subgroup of index $2$, here of order $15$, which is cyclic). If $|G|=120$, $G=S_5$. If $|G|=60$, $G$ has index $2$ in $S_5$, hence is normal, so $G\cap A_5\trianglelefteq A_5$ with $|A_5:G\cap A_5|\le2$; as $A_5$ is simple and has no subgroup of index $2$, $G\cap A_5=A_5$, so $G=A_5$.

Subfields $E$ with $|E:\mathbb{Q}|=2$ correspond to subgroups $H\le G$ of index $2$. Such $H$ is normal with abelian quotient, so $H\supseteq G'$. For $G=A_5$, $G'=A_5$, so no $H$ exists. For $G=S_5$, $G'=A_5$ has index $2$, so $H=A_5$ is the only one. Hence there is at most one such $E$.

**(ii)** $\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]$ and $\mathbb{Q}[\beta]$ are subfields of $S$ of degree $2$ (as $\alpha,\beta\notin\mathbb{Q}$ have degree-2 minimal polynomials $x^2-\alpha^2$, $x^2-\beta^2$). By (i) they are equal, so $\beta=a\alpha+b$ with $a,b\in\mathbb{Q}$. Then $\beta^2=a^2\alpha^2+b^2+2ab\alpha$, so $2ab\alpha\in\mathbb{Q}$, hence $ab=0$ (as $\alpha\notin\mathbb{Q}$). If $a=0$, $\beta=b\in\mathbb{Q}$, a contradiction. So $b=0$, $\beta=a\alpha$ and $\alpha\beta=a\alpha^2\in\mathbb{Q}$. ∎

prompt:
If $K$ is a field, then the general linear group $G=GL_n(K)$ is the multiplicative group of $n\times n$ invertible matrices over $K$.

(i) If the characteristic of $K$ is not equal to $2$, show that $G$ has precisely $n$ conjugacy classes of elements of order $2$.

(ii) If $\mathrm{char}\,K=2$, show that $G$ has precisely $[n/2]$ (the greatest integer in $n/2$) conjugacy classes of elements of order $2$.
answer: Conjugacy in $GL_n(K)$ is similarity. (i) $X^2=I$ with $x^2-1$ separable: $X\sim\mathrm{diag}(-I_r,I_{n-r})$, $1\le r\le n$, distinguished by $r=\mathrm{rank}(I-X)$. (ii) $(X-I)^2=0$: Jordan form with $r$ blocks $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, $1\le r\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, again $r=\mathrm{rank}(I-X)$.

solutions.title: Canonical forms of involutions
solutions.body:
Two invertible matrices are conjugate in $G$ iff they are similar, so we count similarity classes of $X$ with $X^2=I
e X$. Similar matrices have the same rank of $I-X$.

**(i)** $\mathrm{char}K
e2$. $X$ satisfies $x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1)$, a product of distinct linear factors, so $X$ is diagonalizable over $K$ with eigenvalues in $\{1,-1\}$. Thus $X\sim D_r=\mathrm{diag}(-1,\dots,-1,1,\dots,1)$ with $r$ entries $-1$. Since $X
eq I$, $r\ge1$; and $r=\mathrm{rank}(I-D_r)$, since $I-D_r=\mathrm{diag}(2,\dots,2,0,\dots,0)$ and $2
e0$. So $D_1,\dots,D_n$ are pairwise non-similar, each has order exactly $2$, and every involution is similar to one of them: exactly $n$ classes.

**(ii)** $\mathrm{char}K=2$. Now $X^2-I=(X-I)^2=0$, so the minimal polynomial divides $(x-1)^2$; the characteristic polynomial is $(x-1)^n$, which splits over $K$, so $X$ has a Jordan form over $K$ with eigenvalue $1$ and blocks of size $\le2$. Hence $X\sim D_r=\mathrm{diag}(J,\dots,J,1,\dots,1)$ with $r$ copies of $J= egin{pmatrix}1&1\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, where $2r\le n$; and $X
e I$ forces $r\ge1$. Conversely each $D_r$ ($r\ge1$) has $D_r^2=I$ (as $J^2= egin{pmatrix}1&2\0&1\end{pmatrix}=I$) and $D_r
e I$. Finally $I-D_r$ has exactly $r$ nonzero entries, one in each of $r$ distinct rows and columns, so $\mathrm{rank}(I-D_r)=r$, and different $r$ give non-similar matrices. So there are exactly $\lfloor n/2floor$ classes. ∎

prompt: Let $S$ be a commutative integral domain and let $R$ be a subring of $S$ with the same identity $1$. Suppose that there exist finitely many elements $s_1,s_2,\ldots,s_n\in S$ such that $S=s_1R+s_2R+\cdots+s_nR$. Show that $R$ is a field if and only if $S$ is a field.
answer: $S$ is a finitely generated $R$-module, hence integral over $R$. If $R$ is a field, multiplication by $s\ne0$ is an injective $R$-linear map of the finite-dimensional space $S$, hence surjective. If $S$ is a field and $0\ne r\in R$, an integral equation for $r^{-1}$ multiplied by $r^{n-1}$ shows $r^{-1}\in R$.

solutions.title: Integrality
solutions.body:
Since $S$ is a commutative ring that is a finitely generated $R$-module, every $s\in S$ is integral over $R$ (determinant trick / Cayley–Hamilton).

**$R$ a field $\Rightarrow$ $S$ a field.** $S$ is a finite-dimensional $R$-vector space. Let $0\ne s\in S$. The map $\mu_s\colon S\to S$, $t\mapsto st$, is $R$-linear and injective because $S$ is a domain. An injective linear map of a finite-dimensional space is surjective, so $st=1$ for some $t$. Hence $S$ is a field.

(Alternatively: take a monic relation $s^n+r_{n-1}s^{n-1}+\cdots+r_0=0$ of minimal degree; minimality and $S$ being a domain give $r_0\ne0$, and then $s^{-1}=-r_0^{-1}(s^{n-1}+\cdots+r_1)$.)

**$S$ a field $\Rightarrow$ $R$ a field.** Let $0\ne r\in R$. Then $r^{-1}\in S$ is integral over $R$: $(r^{-1})^n+c_{n-1}(r^{-1})^{n-1}+\cdots+c_0=0$ with $c_i\in R$. Multiplying by $r^{n-1}$:
$$r^{-1}=-(c_{n-1}+c_{n-2}r+\cdots+c_0r^{n-1})\in R.$$
So every nonzero element of $R$ is invertible in $R$, and $R$ is a field. ∎
